questions.question:
D1 — Review focus
Project/branch/task: Design review of the User Dashboard plan (review-input.md) on main.
ELI10: I rated this plan 4/10 on design. The biggest gaps: no layout order for the three panels, states named but not described, and no visual tokens. Next I'll make mockups, then go through 7 areas (layout, states, user journey, generic-look risk, design system, responsive/a11y, open decisions). You can narrow that.
Stakes if we pick wrong: If we narrow too much, gaps like mobile layout or modal focus behavior go unspecified and the engineer improvises.
Recommendation: A because the plan has gaps in every area and a full review is cheap.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Pros / cons:
A) All 7 passes (recommended)
  ✅ Covers layout, states, journey, slop, system, responsive and decisions
  ✅ Every gap gets its own decision instead of an engineer guessing later
  ❌ More questions, roughly one per finding, so it takes longer overall
B) Focus on states + layout only
  ✅ Faster, hits the two gaps most likely to ship as broken UI
  ❌ Leaves responsive, a11y and token gaps for implementation to improvise
Net: Full coverage costs a few extra questions; narrowing saves time but leaves known gaps open.

options.label: All 7 passes (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Covers every design dimension with per-issue decisions. ✅ Nothing left for the engineer to guess. ❌ More questions overall.

options.label: States + layout only
options.description: ✅ Faster, targets the gaps most likely to ship broken. ❌ Responsive, a11y and tokens stay unspecified.

questions.question:
Want outside design voices before the detailed review?
D2 — Optional outside design voices
Project/branch/task: Design review of the User Dashboard plan on main.
ELI10: I can get two independent second opinions before the 7 passes: Codex scores the plan against hard design rules, and a separate Claude reviewer checks it for completeness. They catch things one reviewer misses, but they add time.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skipping means findings rest on one reviewer; running adds minutes and may only get one voice if Codex is missing.
Recommendation: B, a taste call with no strong preference. This plan's gaps are concrete enough that one reviewer catches the big ones.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: Cross-model check versus fewer steps to a fixed plan.

options.label: No, proceed without (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Straight into the 7 passes with the approved mockup as anchor. ✅ Fewest steps to a fixed plan. ❌ Findings rest on one reviewer; no cross-model check on slop risk or hierarchy.

options.label: Yes, run outside design voices
options.description: ✅ Codex hard-rule + litmus scorecard plus an independent Claude completeness read. ✅ Disagreements surface with both perspectives in the relevant pass. ❌ Adds a few minutes; Codex may be missing here, in which case only the Claude voice runs and it's tagged single-model.

questions.question:
D3 — Cross-project learnings
Project/branch/task: Design review of the User Dashboard plan on main.
ELI10: gstack can search learnings from your other projects on this machine for patterns that might apply here. Nothing leaves your machine. Good for solo developers; skip it if you work across client codebases that shouldn't mix.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Enabling it on mixed client work could bring one client's patterns into another's review.
Recommendation: A because local cross-project patterns usually help a solo builder and stay on disk.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: More pattern recall versus strict project isolation.

options.label: Enable cross-project (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Reviews can reuse patterns found in your other local projects. ✅ Stays on this machine; nothing is uploaded. ❌ Patterns from unrelated client codebases may leak into this review's context.

options.label: Project-scoped only
options.description: ✅ Strict isolation between codebases, safe for client work. ✅ No chance of irrelevant cross-project noise. ❌ Misses useful patterns you already learned elsewhere on this machine.

questions.question:
D4 — Issue 1: Which panel leads the dashboard?
Project/branch/task: Design review of the User Dashboard plan on main.
ELI10: The plan has three panels but no order. Users scan from the top left, so whatever is there gets noticed. Notifications is the only panel that asks the user to do something. Activity is history. Quick actions are two links.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Unread notifications end up below the fold or tied with history, and users miss what needs their attention.
Recommendation: 1A because Hierarchy as service: put the actionable thing first and keep two links small.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Header actions + notifications-first (recommended)
  ✅ Quick actions sit as a compact button row in the page header next to 'Dashboard'
  ✅ Notifications is the primary, wider column; Activity is the secondary column
  ❌ Activity gets less space, which matters if users mostly come for history
B) Quick actions as a hero strip, then panels
  ✅ 'Open workspace' gets the most prominent spot for users heading to work
  ❌ Two links take a full row of prime space and push notifications down
C) Equal three-panel grid (current implied)
  ✅ Simplest to build, no ranking decision needed now
  ❌ Everything competes, so nothing wins; the classic generic dashboard look
Net: Rank by what the user must act on versus treating all panels as equals.

options.label: 1A Notifications-first (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Quick actions as a compact row in the page header. ✅ Notifications wide primary column, Activity secondary. ❌ Activity gets less room.

options.label: 1B Quick-actions strip first
options.description: ✅ 'Open workspace' is the most prominent element. ❌ Two links eat a full row and push notifications down.

options.label: 1C Equal grid
options.description: ✅ Simplest to build. ❌ No hierarchy; everything competes, generic dashboard look.
